concept: Quantum annealing is schedule-based analog evolution for optimization-like Hamiltonians
summary: Quantum annealing uses quantum fluctuations, commonly through transverse-field-style terms, to explore optimization landscapes while annealing toward a classical cost Hamiltonian. It is related to but not identical with gate-model time-evolution product formulas.
limitations: Quantum annealing commonly targets optimization or ground-state preparation; computing a propagator is only one ingredient of that workflow.
Hardware controls, schedule constraints, and environmental effects affect what an annealing implementation represents.
A closed-system dense reference is insufficient to model an analog device or establish a quantum optimization advantage.
implications: Represent the driver, target, and interpolation schedule explicitly through the selected method contract.
Check supported output and backend capabilities before constructing executable recommendations; distinguish reference simulation from analog hardware execution.
Separate evolution primitives from full optimization workflows, state preparation, measurement, and readout ownership.

evidence.note: Reviews quantum annealing as an optimization and analog quantum computation framework using quantum fluctuations.
Distinguishes AQC, stoquastic AQC, and quantum annealing settings in a broader adiabatic computing review.
